newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - MARCH 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - MARCH 17.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The finance ministry is in the midst of plans to radically alter the face of tax and customs services in an effort to turn around the disappointing course of tax revenues and to effectively deal with tax evasion.

--Greek telecoms organisation OTE is preparing for its second public offer in June, reports say. The offer is expected to be coordinated by the National Bank of Greece on both a domestic and foreign level.
--The Commercial Bank announced profits of 13 billion drachmas for last year, and is expected to double returns this year.
--Absorption rates for the Egnatia Highway project is at the very low level of 5.3 percent, compared to 53 percent for the Patras-Athens-Thessaloniki-Evzones highway.

--The disappointing course of fiscal revenues noted in the last month and fears of a continued discrepancy between targets and returns has created a major issue of whether budget forecats will be met and forced National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou to move ahead with significant changes to tax collecting mechanisms.

--The Bank of Greece is facing an explosion of fluidity of close to 1.5 trillion drachma daily in the banking market. While foreign inflows have stabilised, the increased fluidity is thought to come to a great degree frome the reduced sales of state titles and subsequent increased demands from previous issues.
--The absorption of European Union Community Support Framework Funds in the 1994-1996 period is anything but encouraging with 2.7 billion Ecu being absorbed in 1996, from 2.4 in 1995.
--Plans for the Aheloos river diversion project are well under way and at 38 percent of the cost initially estimated in 1993 under the conservative Constantine Mitsotakis government.
--The 500 biggest commercial enterprises managed last year to increase their profits and turnover to 6.5 million drachmas, despite complaints of a slump in the market.

--Despite credible estimates of a further drop in inlfation in March to 6.2 percent, neither the government nor the Bank of Greece or bankers see a new drop in interest rates that will enable cheaper lending for business.
--New legislation will see the introduction of subsidised insurance premiums for insuring against natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.

--The uncertain course of the economy illustrated by the problems in the execution of the 1997 budget is further compounding problems in the placing of public works projects and procurements contracts.
--The Capital Market Commission has imposed fines of 1.5 billion drachmas on the protagonists of last year's Delta scandal at the Athens bourse. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
